title: King Hui of Liang, Part II

verses.t: Zhuang Bao went to see Mencius and said, "I had an audience with the king, and the king told me that he loves music. I did not know how to answer him. What do you think of loving music?" Mencius said, "If the king loves music very much, then the state of Qi is not far from being well governed!" Another day Mencius had an audience with the king and said, "Your Majesty once told Master Zhuang that you love music. Is that so?" The king changed color and said, "I am not able to love the music of the former kings; I only love the music that is popular in the world today." Mencius said, "If Your Majesty loves music very much, then Qi is not far from being well governed! The music of today is just like the music of antiquity." The king said, "May I hear about this?" Mencius said, "Enjoying music alone, or enjoying it with others: which is more delightful?" "It is better to enjoy it with others." "Enjoying music with a few, or enjoying it with many: which is more delightful?" "It is better to enjoy it with many." "Then let me speak to Your Majesty about music. Suppose Your Majesty is having music played here, and the people hear the sound of your bells and drums and the notes of your pipes and flutes, and they all, with aching heads and knitted brows, say to one another: 'Our king loves his music, but why does he bring us to this extremity? Fathers and sons do not see each other; brothers, wives and children are parted and scattered.' Suppose Your Majesty is hunting here, and the people hear the noise of your carriages and horses and see the beauty of your feathered banners, and they all, with aching heads and knitted brows, say to one another: 'Our king loves his hunting, but why does he bring us to this extremity? Fathers and sons do not see each other; brothers, wives and children are parted and scattered.' The reason is nothing else than that you do not share your enjoyment with the people. Now suppose Your Majesty is having music played here, and the people hear the sound of your bells and drums and the notes of your pipes and flutes, and they all, glad and with joyful faces, say to one another: 'Our king must be free from illness, or how could he have music played?' Suppose Your Majesty is hunting here, and the people hear the noise of your carriages and horses and see the beauty of your feathered banners, and they all, glad and with joyful faces, say to one another: 'Our king must be free from illness, or how could he go hunting?' The reason is nothing else than that you share your enjoyment with the people. If Your Majesty now shares your enjoyment with the people, you will be a true king."

King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that the park of King Wen was seventy li square?" Mencius replied, "So it is recorded." "Was it really as large as that?" "The people still thought it small." "My park is only forty li square, and yet the people think it large. Why is that?" "King Wen's park was seventy li square, but the grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers went there, and so did the catchers of pheasants and hares. He shared it with the people. Was it not right that they should think it small? When I first came to your border, I asked about the chief prohibitions of the state before I dared to enter. I heard that inside the border gates there was a park forty li square, and that whoever killed a deer in it was punished as if he had killed a man. So these forty li square are a pitfall in the middle of the kingdom. Is it not right that the people should think it large?"

King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is there a right way to deal with neighboring states?" Mencius replied, "There is. Only the humane ruler can serve a small state with a large one; thus Tang served Ge, and King Wen served the Kunyi. Only the wise ruler can serve a large state with a small one; thus the Great King [Tai] served the Xunyu, and Goujian served Wu. He who with a large state serves a small one delights in Heaven; he who with a small state serves a large one stands in awe of Heaven. He who delights in Heaven protects the whole world; he who stands in awe of Heaven protects his own state. The Book of Odes says: 'I stand in awe of the majesty of Heaven, and so preserve [my state].'" The king said, "Great words indeed! But I have a weakness: I love valor." Mencius replied, "I ask Your Majesty not to love petty valor. To finger one's sword, glare, and say, 'How dare he face me!' is the valor of a common fellow, fit to take on a single man. I ask Your Majesty to make it greater. The Book of Odes says: 'The king blazed with anger; he marshaled his troops to stop the advance on Ju, to strengthen the blessing of Zhou, and to answer the hopes of the world.' This was the valor of King Wen. King Wen was angry once, and gave peace to all the people of the world. The Book of Documents says: 'Heaven, having sent down the people below, made rulers for them and made teachers for them, saying only that they should help the Lord on High and cherish the people in the four quarters. Whether there are offenders or not, I am here; who under Heaven dares to overstep his will?' When one man was acting tyrannically throughout the world, King Wu was ashamed of it. This was the valor of King Wu. And King Wu too was angry once, and gave peace to all the people of the world. If Your Majesty now were also to be angry once and give peace to all the people of the world, the people's only fear would be that Your Majesty did not love valor."

King Xuan of Qi received Mencius in the Snow Palace. The king said, "Do worthy men also have pleasures like these?" Mencius replied, "They do. When people cannot have them, they criticize their superiors. To criticize one's superiors because one cannot have them is wrong; but for one who is above the people not to share his pleasures with the people is also wrong. When a ruler rejoices in the people's joys, the people rejoice in his joys; when he grieves over the people's sorrows, the people grieve over his sorrows. One who rejoices with the whole world and grieves with the whole world and yet does not become a true king has never existed. Long ago Duke Jing of Qi asked Yanzi, 'I wish to make a tour of Zhuanfu and Chaowu, and then follow the coast southward as far as Langye. What should I do so that my tour may be comparable to the tours of the former kings?' Yanzi replied, 'An excellent question! When the Son of Heaven went to visit the feudal lords, it was called an inspection tour, meaning that he inspected what they guarded. When the feudal lords went to court before the Son of Heaven, it was called reporting on office, meaning that they reported on their duties. Neither was without its purpose. In spring they inspected the plowing and supplied those who lacked seed; in autumn they inspected the harvest and helped those who fell short. A saying of the Xia dynasty went: "If our king does not travel, how shall we get relief? If our king does not take his pleasure, how shall we get help? Each journey, each pleasure, is a model for the feudal lords." Now it is not so. An army marches and eats up the grain; the hungry go without food and the weary go without rest. People look askance and slander one another, and the people turn to wickedness. The king's commands are defied and the people oppressed; food and drink flow away like water. Drifting, lingering, wildness and dissipation: these have become the sorrow of the feudal lords. Following the current downstream and forgetting to return is called drifting; following it upstream and forgetting to return is called lingering; chasing game without ever being satisfied is called wildness; delighting in wine without ever being satisfied is called dissipation. The former kings had no pleasures of drifting and lingering, and no conduct of wildness and dissipation. It is for you, my lord, to choose your course.' Duke Jing was pleased. He issued a great proclamation throughout the state and went out to lodge in the countryside. He then opened the granaries to supply those in want. He summoned the Grand Music Master and said, 'Make me music on the mutual delight of ruler and minister.' That music was the Zhizhao and the Juezhao, whose words say, 'What fault is there in restraining one's lord?' To restrain one's lord is to love one's lord."

King Xuan of Qi asked, "People all tell me to pull down the Hall of Light. Should I pull it down, or leave it?" Mencius replied, "The Hall of Light is the hall of a true king. If Your Majesty wishes to practise true kingly government, do not pull it down." The king said, "May I hear about true kingly government?" Mencius replied, "Long ago, when King Wen governed Qi [the region of Mount Qi], farmers paid one-ninth of their produce; the descendants of officials received hereditary salaries; at the passes and in the markets there was inspection but no taxing; there were no prohibitions on the ponds and weirs; and the punishment of an offender did not extend to his wife and children. An old man without a wife is called a widower; an old woman without a husband is called a widow; an old person without children is called solitary; a young child without a father is called an orphan. These four are the most destitute people in the world, with no one to turn to. When King Wen set up his government and practised humaneness, he always put these four first. The Book of Odes says: 'The rich may get along; but pity the forlorn and the solitary!'" The king said, "Excellent words!" Mencius said, "If Your Majesty thinks them excellent, why do you not put them into practice?" The king said, "I have a weakness: I love wealth." Mencius replied, "Long ago Duke Liu loved wealth. The Book of Odes says: 'He stacked [the grain] and stored it in granaries; he wrapped up dried provisions in sacks and bags. He thought of gathering his people and making them glorious. Then with bows and arrows drawn, with shields, spears and battle-axes raised, he set out on the march.' So those who stayed at home had grain stored in granaries, and those who marched had provisions wrapped up, and only then could he set out on the march. If Your Majesty loves wealth, share it with the people, and what difficulty will there be in your becoming a true king?" The king said, "I have a weakness: I love women." Mencius replied, "Long ago the Great King [Tai] loved women, and he was devoted to his consort. The Book of Odes says: 'Gugong Danfu came in the morning, galloping his horse along the banks of the western rivers to the foot of Mount Qi; and with him came the Lady Jiang, and together they looked for a place to settle.' At that time there were no unhappy unmarried women within doors, and no men without wives outside. If Your Majesty loves women, share this with the people, and what difficulty will there be in your becoming a true king?"

Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi, "Suppose one of Your Majesty's ministers entrusted his wife and children to the care of a friend and went off to travel in Chu, and on his return found that his friend had let his wife and children suffer cold and hunger. What should he do about him?" The king said, "Cast him off." "Suppose the chief criminal judge could not keep his officers in order. What should be done about him?" The king said, "Dismiss him." "Suppose the whole realm within the four borders is not well governed. What should be done about that?" The king turned to his attendants and spoke of other things.

Mencius, having an audience with King Xuan of Qi, said, "When we speak of an ancient state, we do not mean one that has tall trees, but one that has ministers whose families have served it for generations. Your Majesty has no ministers you are close to. Those you promoted yesterday, you do not know today that they are gone." The king said, "How could I have known that they lacked ability, so that I could have avoided them?" Mencius said, "The ruler of a state, in promoting worthy men, should do so as if he had no choice, for he may be causing the low to pass over the honored and the distant to pass over his own kin. Should he not be careful? If those around you all say a man is worthy, that is not enough; if all the great officers say he is worthy, that is not enough; if the people of the state all say he is worthy, then look into it, and if you see that he is worthy, then employ him. If those around you all say a man is unfit, do not listen; if all the great officers say he is unfit, do not listen; if the people of the state all say he is unfit, then look into it, and if you see that he is unfit, then dismiss him. If those around you all say a man deserves death, do not listen; if all the great officers say he deserves death, do not listen; if the people of the state all say he deserves death, then look into it, and if you see that he deserves death, then put him to death. So it is said, 'The people of the state put him to death.' Only by acting in this way can one be father and mother to the people."

King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that Tang banished Jie, and that King Wu struck down Zhou?" Mencius replied, "So it is recorded." "May a minister murder his ruler?" Mencius said, "One who robs humaneness is called a robber; one who robs righteousness is called a ruffian. A man who is a robber and a ruffian is called a mere fellow. I have heard of the punishing of the mere fellow Zhou; I have not heard of the murder of a ruler."

Mencius, having an audience with King Xuan of Qi, said, "To build a great mansion, Your Majesty will certainly have the master of works look for large timbers. When the master of works finds large timbers, Your Majesty is pleased, thinking that he is equal to his task. If the carpenters then hew them down and make them small, Your Majesty is angry, thinking that they are not equal to their task. Now a man studies something in his youth and in his prime wishes to put it into practice. If Your Majesty says to him, 'Set aside for now what you have learned and follow me,' what then? Suppose you had here a piece of uncut jade: even if it were worth ten thousand yi of gold, you would certainly have a jade-cutter carve and polish it. But when it comes to governing the state, you say, 'Set aside for now what you have learned and follow me.' How is that different from teaching the jade-cutter how to carve jade?"

The people of Qi attacked Yan and conquered it. King Xuan asked, "Some tell me not to take it; some tell me to take it. For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots and conquer it in fifty days is beyond human strength. If I do not take it, Heaven will surely send calamity on me. What if I take it?" Mencius replied, "If taking it would please the people of Yan, then take it. Among the ancients there was one who did so: King Wu. If taking it would not please the people of Yan, then do not take it. Among the ancients there was one who acted so: King Wen. When a state of ten thousand chariots attacks another state of ten thousand chariots, and the people come out with baskets of rice and jugs of drink to welcome Your Majesty's army, is there any other reason than that they are escaping from water and fire? If the water grows deeper and the fire grows hotter, they will simply turn elsewhere."

The people of Qi attacked Yan and took it. The other feudal lords were planning to rescue Yan. King Xuan said, "Many of the feudal lords are plotting to attack me. How should I deal with them?" Mencius replied, "I have heard of one who, with only seventy li, governed the whole world: that was Tang. I have never heard of one with a thousand li who was afraid of others. The Book of Documents says: 'Tang's punitive expeditions began with Ge.' The whole world trusted him. 'When he campaigned in the east, the tribes of the west complained; when he campaigned in the south, the tribes of the north complained, saying, "Why does he leave us till last?"' The people looked for him as in a great drought they look for clouds and rainbows. Those going to market did not stop; those plowing in the fields did not change their work. He punished their rulers and consoled their people, and it was like the coming of timely rain, and the people were overjoyed. The Book of Documents says: 'We wait for our lord; when our lord comes we shall revive.' Now the ruler of Yan oppressed his people, and Your Majesty went and punished him. The people thought you were going to rescue them from water and fire, and they came out with baskets of rice and jugs of drink to welcome Your Majesty's army. But if you kill their fathers and elder brothers, put their sons and younger brothers in bonds, destroy their ancestral temples, and carry off their precious vessels, how can that be right? The whole world was already afraid of the strength of Qi. Now you have doubled your territory without practising humane government, and this is what sets the armies of the world in motion against you. If Your Majesty will quickly issue orders to send back the old and the young, stop the removal of the precious vessels, consult with the people of Yan, set up a ruler for them, and then withdraw, you may still be in time to stop it."

There was a clash between Zou and Lu. Duke Mu [of Zou] asked, "Thirty-three of my officers died, and not one of the common people died for them. If I punish them, there are too many to punish; if I do not punish them, they will go on watching their superiors die with hostile eyes and not save them. What should I do?" Mencius replied, "In years of calamity and famine, the old and weak among your people were tossed into the ditches and gullies, and the able-bodied scattered to the four quarters, several thousands of them; while your granaries were full and your treasuries well stocked, and none of your officers reported this to you. That is the superiors being negligent and cruel to those below. Zengzi said, 'Beware, beware! What goes out from you will come back to you.' Now at last the people have had the chance to pay them back. Do not blame them, my lord. If you practise humane government, the people will love their superiors and die for their officers."

Duke Wen of Teng asked, "Teng is a small state, wedged between Qi and Chu. Should I serve Qi, or should I serve Chu?" Mencius replied, "That kind of planning is beyond me. But if you insist, there is one thing: dig your moats deeper, build your walls higher, and guard them together with your people. If you are ready to die and the people do not desert you, then something can be done."

Duke Wen of Teng asked, "The people of Qi are going to fortify Xue, and I am very afraid. What should I do?" Mencius replied, "Long ago, when the Great King [Tai] lived in Bin, the Di tribes invaded it, and he left and went to live at the foot of Mount Qi. He did not choose to do so; he had no alternative. If you do good, then among your descendants in later generations there will surely be one who becomes a true king. A gentleman founds an enterprise and hands down a tradition that can be continued. As for whether it succeeds, that rests with Heaven. What can you do about them, my lord? Only strive to do good."

Duke Wen of Teng asked, "Teng is a small state. Though I exert all my strength to serve the great states, we cannot escape. What should I do?" Mencius replied, "Long ago, when the Great King [Tai] lived in Bin, the Di tribes invaded it. He served them with skins and silks, but could not escape; he served them with dogs and horses, but could not escape; he served them with pearls and jade, but could not escape. Then he gathered his elders and told them, 'What the Di want is our land. I have heard that a gentleman does not let what is meant to nourish people become a cause of harm to them. Why should you worry, my friends, about being without a ruler? I am going to leave.' He left Bin, crossed Mount Liang, and built a town at the foot of Mount Qi and settled there. The people of Bin said, 'He is a humane man; we must not lose him.' Those who followed him were as many as people flocking to market. Others say, 'This is a land that has been guarded for generations; it is not something one man can decide. Be ready to die rather than leave it.' I ask you, my lord, to choose between these two courses."

Duke Ping of Lu was about to go out, when his favorite, a man named Zang Cang, made a request: "On other days when you have gone out, my lord, you have always told the officers where you were going. Today your carriage is already harnessed, and the officers do not yet know where you are going. May I ask?" The duke said, "I am going to see Mencius." "What is this! You lower yourself to pay the first visit to a common man, because you think him worthy? Ritual and righteousness come from worthy men, yet Mencius's funeral for his mother surpassed his funeral for his father. Do not go to see him, my lord." The duke said, "Very well." Yuezhengzi went in to see the duke and said, "Why did you not go to see Meng Ke, my lord?" The duke said, "Someone told me that Mencius's later funeral surpassed the earlier one, so I did not go to see him." Yuezhengzi said, "What do you mean by 'surpassed', my lord? That at the earlier he used the rites of a scholar and at the later those of a great officer, three tripods at the earlier and five at the later?" "No, I mean the fineness of the inner and outer coffins and the grave clothes." "That is not what is called surpassing. It is that his means were different, poor before and rich after." Yuezhengzi went to see Mencius and said, "I spoke to the ruler, and he was going to come to see you. But there is a favorite of his named Zang Cang who stopped him, and so the ruler did not come after all." Mencius said, "When a man goes forward, something may urge him on; when he stops, something may hold him back. But going forward and stopping are not within a man's power. My not meeting the Marquis of Lu is from Heaven. How could the son of the Zang family make me fail to meet him?"
